To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Stem cell lineage specification is directed by the elasticity of the underlying extracellular matrix and is mediated by the Rho/ROCK signaling pathway.
the mechanical properties of the substrate direct stem cell lineage specification and differentiation.
the elastic properties of the extracellular matrix (ECM) are a critical determinant of lineage specification for stem cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of the ECM in stem cell lineage commitment and differentiation.
the role of mechanical forces in the differentiation of human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs).
understanding how cells sense and respond to their mechanical environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MSCs are not stem cells.
there is no evidence of a mesenchymal to endodermal or ectodermal lineage switch.
the expression of genes that indicate mesenchymal lineage is not significantly altered in MSCs plated on compliant gels.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MSC phenotype is not altered by the initial isolation process but rather by the mechanical properties of the matrix.

MSCs are able to sense the mechanical stiffness of their surroundings, which is a function of both their initial isolation and subsequent expansion in culture, and that these cells respond by changing their gene expression patterns.
MSCs are not a homogenous population of cells and are highly plastic in their phenotype.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the matrix elasticity of a culture surface can direct stem cell fate decisions.
the mechanical properties of the matrix are more important than the stiffness of the matrix.
MSCs can be directed toward a particular cell lineage by altering the elasticity of the extracellular environment.
